title: The Nephron and Dialysis
subtitle: Filtration, reabsorption and secretion in the nephron, and how dialysis compares
subject: Biology
syllabusModule: Module 8 Non-infectious Disease and Disorders (2017) + Cells to systems (2025)
syllabusDotPoints: explain a range of causes of disorders by investigating the structures and functions of the relevant organs, for example: loss of kidney function
investigate technologies that are used to assist with the effects of a disorder, including but not limited to: (ACSBL100) loss of kidney function: dialysis
evaluate the effectiveness of a technology that is used to manage and assist with the effects of a disorder (ACSBL100)
Explain how glomerular filtration, selective reabsorption and secretion contribute to the removal of waste in nephrons
Use models to explain how the glomerulus, Bowman’s capsule and nephron tubules contribute to filtration and reabsorption for waste removal in the kidney
Conduct a secondary-source investigation to compare the process of renal dialysis to the function of the kidney
inquiryQuestion: How can technologies be used to assist people who experience disorders?
lessonIntent: Students can explain how glomerular filtration, selective reabsorption and secretion remove waste in the nephron, explain how haemodialysis works, and compare dialysis with kidney function.
examSkill: Describe filtration, selective reabsorption and secretion by site and direction, explain haemodialysis using diffusion and concentration gradients, and compare dialysis with a healthy kidney.
productionNotes: Rewritten for both syllabuses: nephron filtration, selective reabsorption and secretion, plus dialysis compared with kidney function. Causes of kidney failure and transplantation removed (not in the 2025 syllabus). Replaces the earlier Part A/Part B split plan.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, the nephron and how dialysis compares with a working kidney. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: A kidney built from sausage casings
scenes.body: In 1943, a Dutch doctor built the first working dialysis machine from sausage casings, food cans and a car water pump.
scenes.callout: What does a kidney do that is so hard to copy?
scenes.caption: Willem Kolff's 1943 dialysis machine was the first artificial kidney.

voiceover.text: In nineteen forty three, in the occupied Netherlands, a young doctor named Willem Kolff built the world's first working dialysis machine. He made it from sausage casings, food cans, and the water pump from a car, and he used it to try to clean the blood of patients whose kidneys had failed. His first patients died, but in nineteen forty five his machine saved a woman's life, and dialysis has been keeping people alive ever since. So today we'll open up the real kidney to see how its nephrons remove waste, and then ask a fair question. How close does a dialysis machine actually get to doing that job?

scenes.heading: Step one: glomerular filtration
scenes.body: Blood is filtered under pressure from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule.

bullets.text: The glomerulus is a knot of capillaries where blood pressure is high.
Water and small molecules (glucose, amino acids, urea, ions) are forced into Bowman's capsule.
Blood cells and large proteins are too big, so they stay in the blood.

scenes.secondary: The fluid in the capsule is called filtrate. It contains wastes, but also useful substances the body must get back.
scenes.callout: Filtration is by size, not by usefulness.
scenes.caption: Filtration: high pressure forces water and small molecules from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule.

voiceover.text: Let's go inside the kidney's working unit, the nephron. Each kidney holds about a million of them, and each one removes waste in three steps. Step one is glomerular filtration. Blood arrives at the glomerulus, a tight knot of capillaries, under high pressure. That pressure forces water and small molecules, like glucose, amino acids, urea and ions, out of the blood and into a cup shaped structure around it called Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass through, so they stay in the blood. The fluid collected in the capsule is now called filtrate, and here's the catch. Filtration sorts by size, not by usefulness, so the filtrate holds wastes, but also lots of things the body can't afford to lose.

scenes.heading: Steps two and three: reabsorption and secretion
scenes.body: The tubules reclaim what the body needs and add extra wastes to the filtrate.

bullets.text: Selective reabsorption: useful substances move from the filtrate back into the blood.
The proximal tubule reclaims all the glucose and amino acids, and most of the water and ions.
Secretion: extra wastes like hydrogen ions, potassium and some drugs move from the blood into the tubule.
The collecting duct adjusts final water reabsorption, and what remains is urine.

scenes.callout: Reabsorption: filtrate to blood. Secretion: blood to filtrate.
scenes.caption: Reabsorption returns useful substances to the blood; secretion adds extra wastes to the filtrate.

voiceover.text: So step two is selective reabsorption. As the filtrate moves along the tubules, useful substances are moved out of it and back into the blood in the surrounding capillaries. Most of this happens in the proximal tubule, which reclaims all of the glucose and amino acids by active transport, along with most of the water and ions. In fact, over ninety nine percent of the filtered water ends up back in the blood. Further along, the distal tubule and collecting duct fine tune how much water and salt are kept, under hormone control. Step three is secretion, which runs the other way. Extra wastes that weren't filtered, like hydrogen ions, potassium ions and some drugs, are actively moved from the blood into the tubule. That's also how the kidney helps control blood pH. Whatever is left at the end of the collecting duct is urine.

scenes.heading: The words you need
scenes.body: Six terms carry this whole lesson.

bullets.text: Nephron: the functional unit of the kidney, about a million per kidney.
Glomerulus and Bowman's capsule: where blood is filtered under pressure.
Filtrate: the fluid filtered into the nephron, before it becomes urine.
Selective reabsorption: moving useful substances from the filtrate back into the blood.
Secretion: moving extra wastes from the blood into the tubule.
Haemodialysis: removing wastes from blood by diffusion across an artificial semi-permeable membrane.

scenes.callout: Filter by size, reclaim what's useful, secrete the extras.
scenes.caption: Nephron, glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, filtrate, selective reabsorption, secretion, haemodialysis.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the terms. The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, about a million per kidney. The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule are where blood is filtered under pressure. Filtrate is the fluid that's been filtered into the nephron, before it's been processed into urine. Selective reabsorption means moving useful substances from the filtrate back into the blood. Secretion means moving extra wastes from the blood into the tubule. And haemodialysis is removing wastes from the blood by diffusion across an artificial semi permeable membrane, which is where we're heading next.

scenes.heading: How dialysis filters blood
scenes.body: Dialysis replaces filtration by letting wastes diffuse across a semi-permeable membrane down a concentration gradient.

bullets.text: Blood and dialysate flow on opposite sides of a semi-permeable membrane.
Urea and excess ions diffuse from the blood into the dialysate, down their concentration gradients.
Dialysate flows counter-current to the blood, keeping the gradient steep.

scenes.secondary: The dialysate contains normal blood levels of glucose and ions, so those do not diffuse out, while urea, high in the blood and absent from the dialysate, does. Peritoneal dialysis uses the lining of the abdomen as the membrane instead.
scenes.callout: Diffusion does the work; the gradient does the choosing.
scenes.caption: Dialysis removes wastes by diffusion across a semi-permeable membrane; counter-current flow keeps the gradient steep.

voiceover.text: Now the technology. Dialysis relies on one principle you already know, diffusion across a semi permeable membrane. In haemodialysis, the patient's blood is pumped along one side of a membrane inside a machine, while a fluid called dialysate flows along the other side. Urea is high in the blood and absent from fresh dialysate, so it diffuses down its concentration gradient, out of the blood and into the dialysate, which is then thrown away. The dialysate is made with normal blood levels of glucose and ions, so useful substances don't diffuse out, and proteins and cells are too big to cross. And the dialysate flows the opposite way to the blood, called counter current flow, which keeps the gradient steep along the whole membrane. A typical patient does this about three times a week, for around four hours each time.

scenes.heading: Dialysis compared with a working kidney
scenes.body: Dialysis copies the waste removal, but not everything a kidney does.

bullets.text: Both remove urea and excess ions, and both hold back blood cells and proteins.
The kidney works non-stop; haemodialysis runs for a few hours, a few times a week.
The kidney reabsorbs and secretes actively; dialysis relies only on diffusion.
The kidney makes hormones like erythropoietin (EPO); dialysis cannot.

scenes.callout: Dialysis manages kidney failure. It does not replace the kidney.
scenes.caption: Dialysis removes wastes by diffusion, part-time, and cannot make kidney hormones.

voiceover.text: So how does dialysis really compare with a kidney? This is a comparison the syllabus asks for directly. Start with what's the same. Both remove urea and excess ions from the blood, and both hold back blood cells and large proteins. Now the differences. A kidney works continuously, all day and night, while haemodialysis cleans the blood for a few hours, a few times a week, so wastes build up again between sessions. The kidney uses active reabsorption and secretion to adjust exactly what it keeps, but dialysis relies only on diffusion, so what stays in the blood is set by the dialysate recipe. And the kidney makes hormones, like erythropoietin, or E P O, which tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells. Dialysis can't do that. So dialysis manages kidney failure, but it doesn't fully replace the kidney.

scenes.heading: How haemodialysis clears urea
scenes.question: Explain how haemodialysis removes urea from the blood. Refer to the semi-permeable membrane, the concentration gradient, and why the dialysate flows counter-current.
scenes.coachNote: Build the explanation around diffusion: the membrane selects by size, the gradient drives the movement, counter-current keeps the gradient steep.
steps: Blood flows along one side of a semi-permeable membrane and dialysate along the other.
Urea is high in the blood and absent from fresh dialysate, so it diffuses down its gradient across the membrane.
The membrane lets small molecules like urea through, but keeps proteins and blood cells in the blood.
Dialysate flows counter-current, opposite to the blood, so the gradient stays steep along the whole membrane.
Answer: urea diffuses from blood to dialysate down a gradient kept steep by counter-current flow ✓
scenes.caption: Urea diffuses across the membrane down its gradient; counter-current flow keeps that gradient steep.

voiceover.text: Let's build the full explanation of how haemodialysis clears urea, because the marks are in the detail. Frame it around diffusion. Step one, the setup. The patient's blood flows along one side of a semi permeable membrane, and dialysate flows along the other. Step two, the driving force. Urea is high in the blood and absent from fresh dialysate, so it diffuses down its concentration gradient, from the blood into the dialysate. Step three, selectivity. The membrane's pores let small molecules like urea through, but keep proteins and blood cells in the blood. Step four, counter current flow. Because the dialysate runs the opposite way to the blood, fresh dialysate always meets blood that still carries some urea, so the gradient stays steep along the whole membrane. If they flowed the same way, the two sides would even out partway along, and removal would stall.

scenes.heading: Three traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: saying the glomerulus filters out only waste. It filters all small molecules by size, including glucose; the tubules then reabsorb the useful ones.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: mixing up the directions. Reabsorption moves substances from the filtrate into the blood; secretion moves them from the blood into the filtrate. Trap 3: saying dialysis replaces the kidney. It only removes wastes by diffusion, part-time, and cannot make hormones like EPO.
scenes.callout: Filter by size. Reabsorb into blood. Secrete into tubule. Dialysis manages, it doesn't replace.
scenes.caption: The glomerulus filters by size; reabsorption and secretion run in opposite directions; dialysis does not replace the kidney.

voiceover.text: Three traps that cost marks every year. Trap one, saying the glomerulus filters out only the waste. It doesn't know what's waste. It filters every small molecule by size, glucose included, and the tubules then reabsorb the useful ones. Trap two, mixing up the directions. Reabsorption moves substances from the filtrate back into the blood, while secretion moves substances from the blood into the filtrate. Opposite directions, so name the direction every time. Trap three, saying dialysis replaces the kidney. It only removes wastes by diffusion, and only part of the week, and it can't make hormones like E P O. It manages kidney failure rather than curing it.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Dialysate is made with no urea, but with the same glucose and sodium concentrations as normal blood. Explain why each is set this way.
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause and think about the concentration gradients.
answerSteps: Substances diffuse across the membrane only if there is a concentration gradient.
No urea in the dialysate gives a steep gradient, so urea diffuses out of the blood.
Glucose at normal blood level means no gradient, so the patient does not lose glucose.
Sodium at normal level stops too much sodium leaving; only excess sodium diffuses out.
Answer: the dialysate recipe sets the gradients, so wastes leave and useful substances stay ✓
scenes.caption: No urea gives a steep gradient to remove urea; normal glucose and sodium means no net loss.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Dialysate is made with no urea at all, but with the same glucose and sodium concentrations as normal blood. Explain why each is set that way. Pause and think about the concentration gradients. Right, let's check it. Substances only diffuse across the membrane when there's a concentration gradient. With no urea in the dialysate, there's a steep gradient for urea, so it diffuses out of the blood and gets removed. Glucose is set at the normal blood level, so there's no gradient and the patient doesn't lose glucose they need. Sodium works the same way. At a normal level, only excess sodium leaves, rather than the blood being stripped of it. So the dialysate recipe sets the gradients, which is how dialysis does a rough version of what selective reabsorption does in a real nephron.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Filtration: high pressure forces water and small molecules from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule.
Selective reabsorption returns glucose, amino acids, most water and ions from the filtrate to the blood.
Secretion moves extra wastes, like hydrogen and potassium ions, from the blood into the tubule.
Haemodialysis removes urea by diffusion across a membrane, with counter-current flow keeping the gradient steep.
Dialysis is part-time, diffusion only and makes no hormones, so it manages but does not replace the kidney.
scenes.finalPrompt: Comparing dialysis with a kidney? Check what is removed, how, how often, and what dialysis cannot do.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: filtration, reabsorption, secretion, how dialysis works, and how it compares with a kidney.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five takeaways. First, filtration. High pressure forces water and small molecules out of the glomerulus and into Bowman's capsule. Second, selective reabsorption returns glucose, amino acids, and most of the water and ions from the filtrate back to the blood. Third, secretion moves extra wastes, like hydrogen and potassium ions, from the blood into the tubule. Fourth, haemodialysis removes urea by diffusion across a membrane, with counter current flow keeping the gradient steep. And fifth, dialysis only works part time, only uses diffusion and makes no hormones, so it manages kidney failure but doesn't replace the kidney. When you compare the two, check what's removed, how, how often, and what dialysis can't do.
